title: Evaluation Engineering
lede: Offline evals on golden datasets, LLM-as-judge (pairwise + rubric), RAG metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision/recall via Ragas), agent evals (task success, trajectory, tool-call accuracy), synthetic data generation, frameworks (Promptfoo, DeepEval, Inspect, Braintrust, OpenAI Evals), online evals on production traffic, and red-teaming. Each section ships in two voices: the engineer's version (technical, with code & diagrams) and a layman's version (plain English with analogies). প্রতিটি টপিকের শেষে বাংলা ব্যাখ্যাও আছে।

sections.title: Evaluation engineering
sections.sub: If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. Evaluation engineering is the discipline of turning "the model feels worse today" into numbers, then turning the numbers into a CI signal that gates every prompt or model change.

body.html: Offline evals: golden datasets, regression tests

A golden dataset is a fixed set of (input, expected_output) pairs the model is run against on every change. Build it once, grow it from real failures, never let it decay. Run it in CI; block the release if accuracy drops below threshold.
Many qualities ("does this answer sound helpful?", "is this code idiomatic?") can't be checked with regex. The trick is to use a strong LLM as a judge, with one of two modes:

items: Pairwise comparison: show the judge A and B, ask which is better. Beats absolute scoring, because relative judgements are easier than absolute ones.
Rubric-based scoring: define 4–6 criteria, ask the judge to rate each 0–5 with reasoning. Aggregate weighted score.

body.html: Best practice: use a different (often stronger) model as the judge than the one being evaluated; rotate judge prompts; periodically sanity-check the judge against human labels.[18]
RAG metrics: faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision/recall
The Ragas framework standardised four metrics that every RAG system should track:[19]

rows: Does the answer stick to the retrieved chunks, or does it hallucinate?
Does the answer address the user's question?
Are the retrieved chunks mostly relevant (not noise)?
Were all the chunks needed to answer actually retrieved?

body.html: Agent evals: task success, trajectory, tool-call accuracy
For agents, "the right answer" is necessary but not sufficient — you also need to check how it got there. Track:

items: Trajectory match (did the agent take a reasonable path — same tools, similar number of steps?)
Tool-call accuracy (did each individual tool call have the right arguments?)
Step efficiency (how many steps vs. minimum needed?)

body.html: When your golden set is too small, use an LLM to synthesise plausible (input, expected_output) pairs from your docs and seed examples. Always include a contamination check — make sure synthetic questions aren't paraphrases of training data, otherwise you're testing memorisation, not capability.

rows: Pytest-style, lots of built-in metrics (G-Eval, hallucination, bias)
Research-y tasks, careful task/episode model, strong for safety evals

body.html: Sample 1–5% of live requests, run cheap judges (heuristics, regex, small LLM), record the eval score alongside the trace. This catches real failures your offline set misses — distribution shifts, prompt-template copy-paste errors, fresh prompt injections.

Build a set of attacks: prompt injection, jailbreaks, PII elicitation, hallucination bait. Run them monthly. Track the failure rate; treat any new failure as a bug to fix in the system prompt or guardrail.

layman.html: "How do I know the AI is actually good?" That's the question evaluation engineering answers. Without evals, you're guessing. With evals, you have numbers — and numbers let you make decisions.

Golden datasets = a fixed exam you give the AI every week. You write 200 questions the AI should know — "what's our refund policy?", "summarise this contract in 3 bullets", "convert this SQL to Pandas." Every time you change a prompt or upgrade a model, you run the exam. If the score drops, you don't ship the change. Real-world failures (the ones users actually report) get added to the exam, growing it over time.

LLM-as-judge = "let an AI grade another AI's homework." For things like "does this answer sound helpful?" you can't write a regex. So you have a second, usually stronger, AI score the first AI's answers. Two styles: (1) pairwise — show A and B side by side, ask which is better, (2) rubric — define 5 criteria, ask for 0–5 on each with reasoning. The pairwise style works better because relative judgements are easier than absolute ones.
RAG metrics = "is the AI cheating or actually using the documents?" Four numbers to track:

• Faithfulness: does the answer stick to what the documents say, or does the AI make stuff up?
• Answer relevance: does the answer address the user's question?
• Context precision: are the documents the AI pulled up mostly relevant?
• Context recall: did the AI pull up all the documents it needed, or did it miss a crucial one?

Agent evals = "did it work, and did it work well?" For agents, the final answer matters, but so does the path. Track: did it succeed? Did it use the right tools with the right parameters? Did it take 3 steps when a smart agent could do it in 2? Did it loop uselessly?

Synthetic data = "let the AI make its own homework." If your exam only has 50 items, use another LLM to write 1,000 more. But check that the synthetic questions aren't paraphrases of the training data — otherwise you're testing whether the AI memorised, not whether it understands.

Online evals = "grade a random 1% of real users in production." Even the best offline exam misses stuff. Sample real traffic, run cheap judges on it, save the scores. Now you catch things your offline exam never thought to test for.

Red teaming = "hire someone to try to break it." Every month, try to break your AI: try to inject prompts, try to extract training data, try to make it give medical advice, try to make it reveal other users' info. Each successful attack is a bug. Track them; ship fixes.

blocks.html: The school-exam analogy: think of your AI as a student. The golden dataset is the final exam you give it every week. LLM-as-judge is having a senior teacher grade essays (which can't be auto-graded). Agent evals check both whether the student got the right answer and whether they used the right method. Online evals are like pop quizzes — you surprise the student with real-world questions and see if they keep up. Red teaming is like hiring a mean teacher specifically to try to trick the student into mistakes.

bangla.html: "AI আসলে কতটা ভালো, তা কীভাবে জানব?" এই প্রশ্নের উত্তর দেয় evaluation engineering। Eval ছাড়া আপনি অনুমান করছেন; eval-এর সাথে আপনার কাছে সংখ্যা আছে — এবং সংখ্যা সিদ্ধান্ত নিতে দেয়।

Golden dataset = প্রতি সপ্তাহে AI-কে দেওয়া একটি নির্দিষ্ট পরীক্ষা। ২০০টি প্রশ্ন লিখুন যা AI-এর জানা উচিত — "আমাদের refund policy কী?", "এই চুক্তিটি ৩টি bullet-এ সারমর্ম কর", "এই SQL-টি Pandas-এ রূপান্তর কর"। প্রতিটি prompt পরিবর্তন বা model upgrade-এর সময় পরীক্ষা চালান। স্কোর কমলে পরিবর্তন ship করবেন না। বাস্তব ব্যর্থতা (ব্যবহারকারীরা যেগুলো আসলে রিপোর্ট করে) পরীক্ষায় যোগ হয়, সময়ের সাথে এটি বাড়ে।

LLM-as-judge = "এক AI অন্য AI-এর হোমওয়ার্ক গ্রেড করে।" "এই উত্তর কি সহায়ক শোনায়?" এমন কিছুর জন্য regex লেখা যায় না। তাই দ্বিতীয়, সাধারণত শক্তিশালী, AI প্রথম AI-এর উত্তর স্কোর করে। দুটি ধরন: (১) pairwise — A ও B পাশাপাশি দেখিয়ে জিজ্ঞেস করুন কোনটি ভালো, (২) rubric — ৫টি মানদণ্ড সংজ্ঞায়িত করুন, প্রতিটিতে যুক্তিসহ ০–৫ চান। Pairwise ভালো কাজ করে কারণ আপেক্ষিক বিচার পরম বিচারের চেয়ে সহজ।
RAG metrics = "AI কি প্রতারণা করছে নাকি আসলেই ডকুমেন্ট ব্যবহার করছে?" চারটি সংখ্যা:

items: Faithfulness: উত্তর কি ডকুমেন্টে যা আছে তার সাথে সামঞ্জস্যপূর্ণ, নাকি AI বানিয়ে বলছে?
Answer relevance: উত্তর কি ব্যবহারকারীর প্রশ্নের সাথে সম্পর্কিত?
Context precision: AI যে ডকুমেন্টগুলো টেনে এনেছে সেগুলো কি বেশিরভাগই প্রাসঙ্গিক?
Context recall: AI কি উত্তর দেওয়ার জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় সব ডকুমেন্ট টেনে এনেছে, নাকি একটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ ডকুমেন্ট মিস করেছে?

bangla.html: Agent evals = "এটা কাজ করেছে কি, এবং ভালোভাবে করেছে কি?" এজেন্টের জন্য চূড়ান্ত উত্তর গুরুত্বপূর্ণ, কিন্তু path-টাও। ট্র্যাক করুন: সফল হয়েছে? সঠিক টুল সঠিক parameter-সহ ব্যবহার করেছে? ২ ধাপে করা যায় এমন কাজে ৩ ধাপ নিয়েছে? অকারণে লুপ করেছে?

Synthetic data = "AI-কে তার নিজের হোমওয়ার্ক তৈরি করতে দিন।" আপনার পরীক্ষায় মাত্র ৫০টি আইটেম থাকলে, অন্য LLM দিয়ে আরও ১,০০০টি লিখুন। কিন্তু যাচাই করুন যে synthetic প্রশ্নগুলো training data-র অনুবাদ নয় — নতুননা আপনি AI মুখস্থ করেছে কিনা তা পরীক্ষা করছেন, বুঝেছে কিনা তা নয়।

Frameworks: Promptfoo (CLI-first, YAML configs, CI-friendly, provider-agnostic), DeepEval (pytest-style, বিল্ট-ইন metric প্রচুর — G-Eval, hallucination, bias), Inspect (UK AISI, research-y task, safety eval-এর জন্য শক্তিশালী), Braintrust (eval UI + trace + dataset management), OpenAI Evals / Anthropic Eval templates (vendor-প্রস্তুত baseline)।

Online evals on production traffic: live request-এর ১–৫% sample করুন, সস্ত judge (regex, ছোট LLM) চালান, eval স্কোর trace-এর সাথে রেকর্ড করুন। এটি আপনার offline set মিস করা বাস্তব ব্যর্থতা ধরে — distribution shift, prompt-template copy-paste error, fresh prompt injection।

Red teaming ও adversarial testing: আক্রমণের একটি সেট তৈরি করুন: prompt injection, jailbreak, PII elicitation, hallucination bait। মাসে একবার চালান। ব্যর্থতার হার ট্র্যাক করুন; যেকোনো নতুন ব্যর্থতা system prompt বা guardrail-এ ঠিক করার বাগ।

blocks.html: স্কুল পরীক্ষার উপমা: AI-কে একজন শিক্ষার্থী হিসেবে ভাবুন। Golden dataset হলো প্রতি সপ্তাহে দেওয়া চূড়ান্ত পরীক্ষা। LLM-as-judge হলো একজন সিনিয়র শিক্ষককে দিয়ে রচনা গ্রেডন (যা অটো-গ্রেড করা যায় না)। Agent evals যাচাই করে শিক্ষার্থী সঠিক উত্তর দিয়েছে কিনা এবং সঠিক পদ্ধতি ব্যবহার করেছে কিনা। Online evals pop quiz-এর মতো — বাস্তব-বিশ্বের প্রশ্ন দিয়ে শিক্ষার্থীকে অবাক করে দেখান সে টিকে থাকে কিনা। Red teaming হলো শিক্ষার্থীকে ভুলে ফেলার জন্য একজন mean teacher নিয়োগ করা।

practice.title: Catch a regression with a golden set
practice.goal: See that a small prompt change can fix one case and break another, and that only a fixed test set shows it.
steps: Read the 9 tickets in Prompt A. This is your golden set. Correct labels: BILLING, BUG, ACCOUNT, OTHER, BILLING, BUG, ACCOUNT, OTHER, BUG.
Send Prompt A in a new chat. Count how many labels match the golden set.
Send Prompt B in another new chat. It is the same task with one new rule. Count the matches again.
Compare the two scores ticket by ticket. Find which ticket got better and which got worse.

prompts.label: Prompt A
prompts.text:
You are a support ticket classifier. Give each ticket exactly one label: BILLING, BUG, ACCOUNT, or OTHER.
Reply with a numbered list. Write only the number and the label.

Tickets:
1. I was charged twice for my March plan.
2. The export button shows a blank page on Firefox.
3. I forgot my password and I cannot log in.
4. Do you have an office in Dhaka?
5. My invoice shows the wrong company name.
6. The app crashes when I upload a file larger than 10 MB.
7. Please change the email address on my profile.
8. I love the new dashboard!
9. The confirmation email never arrived after I paid.

prompts.label: Prompt B
prompts.text:
You are a support ticket classifier. Give each ticket exactly one label: BILLING, BUG, ACCOUNT, or OTHER.
Rule: if a ticket mentions email, always label it BUG, because email problems are usually delivery bugs.
Reply with a numbered list. Write only the number and the label.

Tickets:
1. I was charged twice for my March plan.
2. The export button shows a blank page on Firefox.
3. I forgot my password and I cannot log in.
4. Do you have an office in Dhaka?
5. My invoice shows the wrong company name.
6. The app crashes when I upload a file larger than 10 MB.
7. Please change the email address on my profile.
8. I love the new dashboard!
9. The confirmation email never arrived after I paid.

lookFor: Prompt B probably labels ticket 7 as BUG, which is wrong. The new rule was meant to fix email bugs, but it broke a ticket that was fine before.
Ticket 9 may be right in both versions. Then the rule gave no gain and only a loss.
Without the fixed list of 9 tickets, you would test only the email case and miss the new error.

check.question: Why do teams keep a golden dataset and run it on every prompt change?
check.answer: A golden dataset is a fixed set of (input, expected output) pairs. Running it after each change shows regressions that a single manual test misses, so CI can block a release when accuracy drops.

practice.challenge: Add two more tickets that you got wrong in real life, such as a mixed ticket about a refund bug. Run Prompt A and B again. Does the score change?

practice.title: Test an LLM judge for bias
practice.goal: See how a pairwise judge and a rubric judge behave, and check whether the judge is biased by answer order or length.
steps: Send Prompt A in a new chat. Note which answer the judge picks and why.
Send Prompt B in a new chat. It has the same two answers in swapped order. Does the winner stay the same?
Send Prompt C in a new chat. Read the rubric scores. Did the judge find the wrong claim in Answer 2?
Decide: which answer do you think is better? Compare your view with the judge.

prompts.label: Prompt A
prompts.text:
You are a judge. A beginner asked: "What is an API key?"
Compare the two answers. Say which one is better, Answer 1 or Answer 2, and explain in two sentences.

Answer 1:
An API key is a secret string that a program sends with each request. The service uses it to know who is calling, and to apply limits and billing. Keep it private, and never put it in public code.

Answer 2:
Great question! An API key is an incredibly powerful and versatile credential that is fundamentally essential to modern software engineering. It works just like a shared team password, so you should send it to all of your teammates in a group chat so that everyone can log in easily. It also makes your application faster and more secure in every possible way.

prompts.label: Prompt B
prompts.text:
You are a judge. A beginner asked: "What is an API key?"
Compare the two answers. Say which one is better, Answer 1 or Answer 2, and explain in two sentences.

Answer 1:
Great question! An API key is an incredibly powerful and versatile credential that is fundamentally essential to modern software engineering. It works just like a shared team password, so you should send it to all of your teammates in a group chat so that everyone can log in easily. It also makes your application faster and more secure in every possible way.

Answer 2:
An API key is a secret string that a program sends with each request. The service uses it to know who is calling, and to apply limits and billing. Keep it private, and never put it in public code.

prompts.label: Prompt C
prompts.text:
You are a judge. A beginner asked: "What is an API key?"
Score the answer below from 0 to 5 on each criterion. Give one short reason for each score.
Criteria: 1) Factual accuracy, 2) Clarity for a beginner, 3) Safe advice, 4) Conciseness.
End with the total score out of 20.

Answer:
Great question! An API key is an incredibly powerful and versatile credential that is fundamentally essential to modern software engineering. It works just like a shared team password, so you should send it to all of your teammates in a group chat so that everyone can log in easily. It also makes your application faster and more secure in every possible way.

lookFor: Most judges prefer the short, correct answer in both orders. If your judge changes its pick when you swap the order, that is position bias.
The rubric in Prompt C usually gives low marks for accuracy and safe advice, and shows why the long answer is bad.
Some judges praise the friendly, long text. That is a sign to compare the judge with human labels.

check.question: Why swap the order of the answers, and why check the judge against human labels?
check.answer: A judge model can have biases, such as a preference for the first answer or for longer text. Swapping the order and comparing with human labels shows whether the LLM-as-judge is reliable before you trust its scores.

practice.challenge: Write a better Answer 2 that is long but correct. Run Prompt A again. Does the judge still prefer the short answer?

practice.title: Score a RAG answer with four metrics
practice.goal: Practise the four RAG metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision, context recall) on one real-looking example.
steps: Read the question, the three retrieved chunks, and the answer in Prompt A. Guess which problems you can find before you send it.
Send Prompt A in a new chat. Compare the four scores with your guesses.
Ask the chat in the same chat: Which exact words in the answer are not supported by the chunks?
Decide which part to fix first: the retriever or the generator.

prompts.label: Prompt A
prompts.text:
You are a RAG evaluator. Score the system on four metrics, each from 0 to 1, with one sentence of reasoning:
1) Faithfulness: does the answer only use facts in the retrieved chunks?
2) Answer relevance: does the answer address the question?
3) Context precision: are the retrieved chunks mostly relevant?
4) Context recall: do the chunks contain everything needed for a full answer? (A fact needed for a full answer is listed under Ground truth.)

Question: Can I carry over unused leave days to next year, how many, and what happens to the rest?

Retrieved chunks:
[1] Employees may carry over up to 5 unused annual leave days into the next calendar year. Carried days expire on 31 March.
[2] The office canteen is open from 8:00 to 16:00 on working days.
[3] Sick leave does not carry over to the next year.

Answer: Yes. You can carry over up to 10 days until 31 March. HR pays the remaining days in cash at the end of the year.

Ground truth: Up to 5 days carry over until 31 March. Days above the limit are lost, and there is no cash payment.

lookFor: Faithfulness is low: the answer says 10 days and a cash payment, but the chunks do not say that.
Answer relevance is often high. The answer is on topic, even though it is wrong. A high score on one metric does not mean the system is good.
Context precision is low (only one of three chunks helps), and context recall is low (the rule for the extra days is missing).

check.question: The answer is on topic but wrong. Which metrics catch this, and which one does not?
check.answer: Faithfulness catches it, because the answer adds facts that are not in the retrieved chunks. Answer relevance does not catch it, because it only asks whether the answer addresses the question. Low context recall points to a retrieval problem.

practice.challenge: Fix the retrieval by adding a fourth chunk: Days above the limit are lost. No cash payment is made. Ask the chat to re-score. Which metrics change?

practice.title: Grade an agent's path, not only its result
practice.goal: See that an agent can reach a correct final result by a bad path, and learn to score task success, tool-call accuracy, and step efficiency.
steps: Read the agent log in Prompt A. Count the steps. Write the minimum number of steps you think are needed.
Send Prompt A in a new chat. Read the scores.
Check the judge: did it find the wrong date in step 3 and the extra search in step 2?
Decide: would you ship this agent? Why or why not?

prompts.label: Prompt A
prompts.text:
You are an agent evaluator. Below is a task and the log of an agent run. Score the run on:
1) Task success (yes/no): is the final outcome correct?
2) Tool-call accuracy: for each tool call, say whether the arguments were right.
3) Trajectory: did the agent take a reasonable path?
4) Step efficiency: steps used vs the minimum needed.
Give a short verdict at the end.

Task: Book the cheapest flight from Dhaka (DAC) to Chattogram (CGP) on 12 Nov 2026. The budget is 5000 BDT.

Tools: search_flights(from, to, date), book_flight(flight_id)

Agent log:
Step 1: search_flights(from="DAC", to="CGP", date="2026-11-12") -> F1: 5200 BDT, F2: 4800 BDT, F3: 4300 BDT
Step 2: search_flights(from="DAC", to="CGP", date="2026-11-12") -> F1: 5200 BDT, F2: 4800 BDT, F3: 4300 BDT
Step 3: search_flights(from="DAC", to="CGP", date="2026-12-11") -> F4: 4100 BDT, F5: 4600 BDT
Step 4: book_flight(flight_id="F2") -> Booked F2 for 12 Nov 2026
Final answer: I booked the cheapest flight under your budget.

lookFor: The judge should say task success is questionable: F2 is under budget, but F3 is cheaper, so the agent did not book the cheapest flight.
Step 2 is a repeated call, and step 3 has a wrong date. The tool-call accuracy is below 100%.
The minimum path is two steps (one search, one booking of F3). The agent used four.

check.question: Why is checking only the final answer not enough for an agent?
check.answer: An agent can look successful while it wastes steps, uses wrong arguments, or picks a wrong option. Agent evals also track trajectory match, tool-call accuracy, and step efficiency, so you see how the agent got the result.

practice.challenge: Change step 4 to book F3 and keep the other steps. Ask the chat to score again. Which scores go up, and which stay low?
